ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
“It may be said that natural selection is daily and hourly 
scrutinizing, throughout the world, every variation, even 
the slightest; rejecting that which is bad, preserving and 
adding up all that is good; silently and insensibly working, 
whenever and wherever opportunity offers, at the 
improvement of each organic being in 
relation to its organic and inorganic 
conditions of life. We see nothing of these 
slow changes in progress, until the hand of 
time has marked the long lapse of ages, 
and then so imperfect is our view into long 
past geological ages, that we only see that 
the forms of life are now different from what 
they formerly were.” 
-- Charles Darwin On the Origin of Species
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Historical Darwin quotation with portrait.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Charles Darwin
● English naturalist
● Most notable research was done at the 
Galapagos Islands
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Darwin voyage map highlights the Galápagos route.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Charles Darwin’s Research
● Darwin was interested in biogeography
○ The geographic distribution of species
● Darwin’s hypothesis:
○ Organisms left South 
America and colonized 
the Galapagos Islands 
where they then 
diversified and gave rise 
to new species
○ Darwin was specifically 
interested in finches
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Finch photographs accompany a biogeography and diversification example.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
True or False?
Before we delve into the theories of natural selection 
and descent with modification, let’s play a game of 
true or false. 
Game Play:
You will be given a total of FOUR statements. You 
and a partner must decide if the statement is true or 
false. Once you choose, you must then try to justify 
your logic.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Statement 1
● Natural selection gives organisms what they need 
to survive
○ FALSE: natural selection has no knowledge of 
what organisms “need.” Natural selection 
simply acts on genetic variations that lead to 
survival and reproduction
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Statement 2
● Natural selection acts for the good of a species
○ FALSE: Natural selection has no intentions. It 
only acts on traits that lead to survival and 
reproduction. 
■ Just because a trait leads to survival doesn’t 
mean it’s good for the species. 
■ For example, let’s say we have a species of 
predators that have a trait that makes them the 
BEST predator, over time they will eat all of 
their prey! If they run out of a food source, they 
will starve and die!
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Statement 3
● Natural selection is a process involving 
organisms trying to adapt to their surroundings
○ FALSE: Natural selection acts on random 
mutations that have lead to a genetic variation 
in the population.
○ Organisms cannot close their eyes and cross 
their fingers and make a wish to adapt
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Statement 4
● “Survival of the fittest” is a common phrase you 
may have heard. The term “fittest” refers to the 
organisms in a population that are the strongest, 
healthiest, and fastest.
○ FALSE: the fittest organism simply refers to 
the organism that (you guessed it) can survive 
and reproduce
■ For example, sickle cell anemia is a trait that 
leads to protection against malaria. But 
individuals with sickle cell anemia would not 
be classified as healthy
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Text-based misconception check uses sickle-cell/malaria as the fitness example; canonical correction distinguishes heterozygote advantage from sickle-cell disease.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Evolution
During his studies, Darwin proposed the idea of 
descent with modification, which is now our modern 
definition of evolution
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Evolution
Evolution: change in the genetic makeup of a 
population over time; descent with modification
● Heritable traits change from generation to 
generation
○ To explain the pattern of descent with 
modification (evolution) he observed, Darwin 
proposed the idea of natural selection
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
● Natural selection: A process in which individuals that 
have certain traits tend to survive and reproduce at 
higher rates than other individuals because of those 
traits
○ Natural selection acts on phenotypic variations in 
populations
■ Some phenotypes will increase or decrease an 
organism’s fitness (ability to survive and 
reproduce)
● Measured by reproductive success 
■ Environments can change, causing selective 
pressures to populations
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
The theory of natural selection is based on two main 
observations that Darwin made:
1. Traits are heritable
2. More offspring are produced than can survive
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
1. Traits are heritable
● Characteristics can be passed from parent to 
offspring
● Adaptations: inherited characteristics of organisms 
that enhance their survival and reproduction
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
2. More offspring are produced than can survive
● This leads to competition for limited resources, 
which results in differential survival
● The traits that lead to survival (“favorable” 
traits) will accumulate in the population
● Populations evolve, NOT individuals
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Artificial Selection
● At the time, Darwin was worried about other 
scientists supporting his work. So he compelled 
them by comparing natural selection to artificial 
selection
○ Artificial selection: the selective breeding of 
domesticated plants and animals to encourage 
the occurrence of desirable traits
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural vs Artificial Selection
● Nature “selects” 
traits that are better 
suited for survival 
and reproduction
● Humans select 
traits that are 
desirable
● Domestication of 
plants and animals
Natural Selection Artificial Selection
Note: Both can lead to evolutionary change in the 
organism, but natural selection occurs in nature 
without the influence of humans
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Practice Problem
A population of pacas, a nocturnal rodent, live in South America. 
Their diet consists of leaves, flowers, and fruits that have fallen 
from taller trees. A recent fire has wiped out much of the food that 
the pacas eat. This has caused the pacas to lose body mass. 
Due to the lack of food, subsequent generations of pacas are 
thinner than the preceding generations. Identify if this is an 
example of descent with modification and justify your response.
No, this is not an example of descent with 
modification because the change that the pacas 
are experiencing is due to an environmental 
influence. The lack of food is causing them to 
be smaller in size. The frequency of their genes 
has not changed. If the food supply were to 
increase, they would simply return to their 
normal body weight. Nature is not selecting for 
anything because there is NO trait to select for.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Population Genetics
● Population: a group of individuals of the same 
species that live in the same area and interbreed 
to produce fertile offspring
○ Gene pool: a population’s genetic makeup
■ Consists of all copies of every type of allele
● If there is only one allele present for a 
particular locus in the population it is fixed
● Many fixed alleles=less genetic diversity

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Population Genetics
● A population’s allele frequencies will change over 
time
○ Remember: populations evolve NOT 
individuals
○ Microevolution: small scale genetic changes 
in a population
■ Evolution is driven by random occurrences
● Mutations
● Genetic Drift
● Migration/gene flow
● Natural selection
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Mutations
● Review: define mutations in your own words
● Mutations can result in genetic variation
○ Can form new alleles
○ Natural selection can act on varied phenotypes
○ Mutation rates tend to be slow in plants and 
animals and fast in prokaryotes due to a faster 
generation time
Note: Mutations can be harmful, neutral, or 
beneficial. Most mutations are in the neutral to 
harmful range. Not all mutations lead to evolution.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Genetic Drift
● Genetic drift: chance events that cause a 
change in allele frequency from one generation to 
the next 
○ Most significant to small populations
○ Can lead to a loss of genetic variation
○ Can cause harmful alleles to become fixed
○ Does NOT produce adaptations
○ Two types:
■ Bottleneck effect
■ Founder effect
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Bottleneck Effect
● Bottleneck effect: when a 
large population is 
drastically reduced by a 
non-selective disaster
○ Floods, famine, fires, 
hurricanes, hunting, etc.
○ Some alleles may 
become 
overrepresented, 
underrepresented, or 
absent
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bottleneck-effect diagram visually narrows a large population to a small surviving sample.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Founder Effect
● Founder effect: when 
a few individuals 
become isolated from 
a large population 
and establish a new 
small population with 
a gene pool that 
differs from the large 
population
○ Lose genetic 
diversity
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Founder-effect diagram shows a small subset establishing a new population.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Gene Flow
● Gene flow: the transfer of alleles into or out of a 
population due to fertile individuals or gametes
○ Alleles can be transferred between populations
■ Example: pollen being blown to a new location
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
Examine each scenario and determine if it is an 
example of the bottleneck effect, founder effect, or 
genetic drift. Justify each response with an 
explanation.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Scenario 1
The black robin is a small bird 
native to the Chatham Islands in 
New Zealand. Before the 19th 
century, much of their habitat was 
converted to farmland.
Due to the loss of their habitat and the introduction of 
non-native predators (like cats), the population declined 
to its lowest point, only 5 individuals. Since then, 
conservation efforts have brought the population 
number back up to an estimated 230 individuals.
Bottleneck effect due to human activity
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Black robin photograph accompanies the severe bottleneck example.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Scenario 2
In the 1720’s an Amish population settled into 
Pennsylvania. A small number of the early settlers 
were from Germany and carried an unusual number 
of mutations, one of which included polydactyly. The 
trait for polydactyly is now much more common in 
the Amish population than it is in the general 
population.
Founder effect
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Scenario 3
Recurrent flash floods have caused mass mortalities 
in the marble trout population. Scientists have 
analyzed the genetic makeup of the remaining 
marble trout population and have found that genetic 
diversity has decreased significantly.
Bottleneck effect
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Scenario 4
Due to an increase in wind in a local area, pollen 
from one population of flowers has travelled further 
than usual and pollinated another population of 
flowers. The offspring of these flowers now have 
traits of each population.
Gene flow
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
Now that you are familiar with natural selection, let’s 
look closer at how it can affect a population
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
● Reproductive success is measured by relative 
fitness
○ The number of surviving offspring that an 
individual produces compared to the number left 
by others in the population
● Effects of natural selection can be measured by 
examining the changes in the mean of phenotypes
○ There are three modes of natural selection
1. Directional selection
2. Stabilizing selection
3. Disruptive selection
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Modes of Natural Selection
Selection 
towards one 
extreme 
phenotype
Selection 
towards the 
mean and 
against the 
extreme 
phenotypes
Selection against 
the mean. Both 
phenotypic 
extremes have 
the highest 
relative fitness
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Three selection-distribution diagrams show directional, stabilizing, and disruptive selection.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Natural Selection
● Sexual selection: a type of natural selection that 
explains why many species have unique/showy 
traits
○ Males often have useless structures (ie 
colorful male peacock feathers) simply 
because females choose that trait
○ Can produce traits that are harmful to survival
■ Example: colorful feathers in male peacocks 
make them easier to spot by predators
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium
● A model used to assess whether natural selection 
or other factors are causing evolution at a 
particular locus
○ Determines what the genetic make up of the 
population would be if it were NOT evolving
■ This is then compared to actual data:
● If there are NO differences, then the 
population is NOT evolving
● If there ARE differences, then the 
population MAY BE evolving
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium
● The Hardy Weinberg principle states:
○ The frequencies of alleles and genotypes in a 
population will remain constant from 
generation to generation, provided that only
Mendelian segregation and recombination of 
alleles are at work
Remember: this is a hypothetical situation where 
no evolution would take place. In real populations 
the allele and genotype frequencies DO change 
over time
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium
● Five conditions must be met to be in Hardy Weinberg 
equilibrium:
1. No mutations
2. Random mating
3. No natural selection
4. Extremely large population size
5. No gene flow
● If any of these conditions are not met, then 
microevolution occurs (i.e. mutation, gene flow, 
genetic drift, natural selection, and non-random 
mating).
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Think, Pair, Share
● Discuss with a partner how each of the five Hardy 
Weinberg conditions, if not met, can lead to 
evolution
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium
● Two formulas: 
Frequency of 
the dominant 
allele in a 
population
Frequency of the 
recessive allele in 
a population
Percentage of 
the homozygous 
dominant 
individuals
Percentage of 
the heterozygous 
individuals
Percentage of 
the homozygous 
recessive 
individuals
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Hardy-Weinberg equations p + q = 1 and p² + 2pq + q² = 1 are visually annotated with allele- and genotype-frequency meanings.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Check
1. You are told that 20% of a population is 
homozygous recessive. What variable is that 
referring to in the Hardy Weinberg equations?
a. It refers to q2
2. You are told that the frequency of a dominant 
allele in a population is 75%. What variable is that 
referring to in the Hardy Weinberg equations?
a. It refers to p
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg Equilibrium
● Which formula you start with depends on the 
information you are given.
● If a problem gives “allele frequencies,” it is referring 
to “p” and “q.” If it gives information about individual 
organisms or populations, then it is referring to p2, 2pq 
and q2
○ Most times you will use both formulas to complete 
the problem
○ Usually you are given q, and then you will need to 
find p, but you will also see problems where that is 
not the case
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Tips For Solving Problems
1. Always write down both equations
2. Identify the information given. Is it for alleles? For 
populations?
3. Regardless of what the problem asks, solve for 
both p and q first, because that will allow you to 
answer any question!
4. Use your calculator to do the square and square 
root functions! The most common mistake 
students make is assuming they know the 
answer.
5. Double check your work
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Hardy Weinberg
Let’s watch a video by Mr. Anderson and see some 
Hardy Weinberg problems being solved, then we will 
practice some problems on our own!

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
1. What is the difference between genotype 
frequencies and allele frequencies in a population?
a. Answer: genotype frequencies refer to how alleles 
combine. Allele frequencies refer to an allele’s 
relative distribution in the population (ie how 
common is the allele).
2. Hardy Weinberg equilibrium is often referred to as a 
null model of evolution. What does this mean?
a. Answer: a null model of evolution is one where no 
evolution occurs, which is assumed with Hardy 
Weinberg if all conditions are met
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Variations in Populations
● The more genetic diversity in a population, the 
better it can respond to changes in the 
environment
○ More likely to be individuals that can withstand 
changes
■ Species with low genetic diversity are at risk of 
decline and/or extinction
● Example: due to poaching and poisoning, the 
California Condor was reduced to 27 
individuals. This drastically lowered the gene 
pool. Even though restoration efforts have 
increased numbers, they have lost diversity
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: California condor example connects a severe demographic decline with loss of genetic diversity.
Blank or section-separator slide with no substantive parsed text.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Evidence of Evolution
● Overwhelming evidence supports the theory of 
evolution
● Primary sources of evidence are:
○ The fossil record
○ Comparative morphology
○ Biogeography
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Fossil Record
● Fossils: remains or traces of past organisms
○ Fossil record: gives a visual of evolutionary 
change over time
■ Fossils can be dated by examining the rate of 
carbon 14 decay and the age of rocks where the 
fossils are found
■ Gives geographical data for the organisms found
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Fossil imagery and dating context accompany fossil-record evidence.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Comparative Morphology
● Comparative morphology: analysis of the 
structures of living and extinct organisms
○ Homology: characteristics in related species that 
have similarities even if the functions differ
■ Embryonic homology: many species have similar 
embryonic development
■ Vestigial structures: structures that are 
conserved even though they no longer have a 
use
● Example: tailbone and appendix in humans
■ Molecular homology: many species share similar 
DNA and amino acid sequences
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Comparative Morphology
○ Homologous 
structures:  
characteristics that are 
similar in two species 
because they share a 
common ancestor
■ Example: arm bones 
of many species
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Comparative forelimb diagram supports homologous-structure reasoning.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Comparative Morphology
● Convergent evolution: similar adaptations that 
have evolved in distantly related organisms due 
to similar environments
○ Analogous structures: structures that are 
similar but have separate evolutionary origins
■ Example: wings in birds vs bats vs bees
● Each species have wings, but the wings did 
not originate from a common ancestor
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bird, bat, and insect wing examples illustrate convergence while the canonical lock preserves homologous tetrapod forelimb ancestry.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Comparative Morphology
● Structural evidence indicates common ancestry
of all eukaryotes
○ Many fundamental and cellular features and 
processes are conserved across organisms
■ Cellular examples:
● Membrane-bound organelles
● Linear chromosomes
● Introns in genes
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cellular-feature list highlights membrane-bound organelles, linear chromosomes, and introns as common-ancestry evidence.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Biogeography
● Biogeography: the distribution of animals and 
plants geographically
○ Example: Species on oceanic islands 
resemble mainland species
○ Example: species on the same continent are 
similar and distinct from species on other 
continents
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
1. What type of data provides evidence for 
evolution?
a. Answer: fossil data, biogeography, and 
morphology
2. In terms of natural selection, how can structures 
become vestigial?
a. Answer: a structure may have been useful at 
one time, but maybe there was a mutation that 
rendered it useless. Therefore it was 
conserved across generations, neither being 
selected for or against
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Putting It All Together
● Populations continue to evolve
○ Genomes change
■ Examples: 
● Antibiotic resistance in bacteria
● Insect resistance to pesticides
● Pathogens cause emerging (new) diseases
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.
Blank or section-separator slide with no substantive parsed text.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Phylogeny
● Systematics: classification of 
organisms and determining 
their evolutionary 
relationships
○ Taxonomy: naming and 
classifying species
○ Phylogenetics: 
hypothesis of evolutionary 
history
■ Use phylogenetic trees to 
show evolution
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Phylogeny
● To determine evolutionary 
relationships, scientists use:
○ Fossil records
○ DNA 
○ Proteins
○ Homologous structures
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Slide contains 1 embedded visual element(s) supporting the displayed instructional content.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Phylogenetic Trees
● Phylogenetic trees: diagrams that represent the 
evolutionary history of a group of organisms
○ Similar to cladograms, except trees show the 
amount of change over time measured by 
fossils
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Phylogenetic-tree illustration accompanies the distinction between scaled trees and cladograms.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cladograms
● Each line represents a lineage
● Each branching point is a node
○ Nodes represent common ancestors
■ Nodes and all branches from it are called clades
■ Species in a clade have shared derived features
○ The root is the common ancestor of all the 
species
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cladogram labels lineages, nodes, clades, shared derived features, and root.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cladograms
● Two clades that emerge from the same node are 
sister taxa
● A lineage that evolved from the root and remains 
unbranched is the basal taxon
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cladogram relationship diagram introduces sister taxa and an early-branching/basal lineage.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cladograms
● Synapomorphy: a derived character shared by 
clade members
○ Derived characteristic: similarity inherited from 
the most recent common ancestor of an entire 
group
○ Ancestral characteristic: similarity that arose 
prior to the common ancestor
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Character mapping on a cladogram supports shared-derived-character reasoning.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Cladograms
● Many cladograms and trees include an outgroup
○ A lineage that is the least closely related to the 
rest of the organisms
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cladogram includes an outgroup used to polarize character states.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Groups
● Monophyletic group:  includes 
the most recent common 
ancestor of the group and all of 
its descendants (clade)
● Paraphyletic group:  includes 
the most recent common 
ancestor of the group, but not all 
its descendants
● Polyphyletic group:  does not 
include the most recent common 
ancestor of all members of the 
group
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Three diagrams compare monophyletic, paraphyletic, and polyphyletic groupings.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Parsimony
● If there are conflicts among characters, use the 
principle of parsimony
○ Use the hypothesis that requires the fewest 
assumptions (DNA changes)
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

a. Answer: beetles
3. What is an example of a sister taxa?
a. Answer: butterflies, moths, and flies

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Speciation
● Species: a group able to interbreed and produce 
viable, fertile offspring
○ Speciation: formation of new species
■ Results in diversity of life forms
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Speciation
● Geography has an impact on speciation
○ Two modes of speciation
■ Allopatric speciation
■ Sympatric speciation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Speciation
● Physical barrier divides 
population or a small 
population is separated 
from main population
● Populations are 
geographically isolated
○ Prevents gene flow
○ Often caused by 
natural disasters
● A new species 
evolves while still 
inhabiting the same 
geographic region as 
the ancestral species
○ Usually due to the 
exploitation of a 
new niche
Allopatric speciation Sympatric speciation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Side-by-side allopatric and sympatric speciation descriptions emphasize geographic isolation versus geographic overlap.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text: Speciation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Four-step visual model contrasts allopatric barrier formation with sympatric divergence and eventual reproductive isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Speciation
● Speciation occurs due to reproductive isolation
○ Two types:
■ Prezygotic barriers
■ Postzygotic barriers
○ Both types maintain isolation and prevent gene 
flow between the populations
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Prezygotic barriers: prevent mating or hinder 
fertilization
○ Five types:
■ Habitat isolation
■ Temporal isolation
■ Behavioral isolation
■ Mechanical isolation
■ Gametic isolation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Habitat isolation: Species live in different areas 
or they occupy different habitats within the same 
area
○ Example: in western North America the mountain 
bluebird lives at high elevation while the eastern 
bluebird lives at low elevation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Bluebird habitat/elevation example illustrates habitat isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Temporal isolation: species breed at different 
times of the day, year, or season
○ Example: the western spotted skunk mates in 
late summer, while the eastern spotted skunk 
mates in late winter
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Spotted-skunk breeding-time example illustrates temporal isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Behavioral isolation: unique behavioral patterns 
and rituals separate species
○ Example: the blue footed boobies will only 
mate after a courtship ritual
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Blue-footed booby courtship example illustrates behavioral isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Mechanical isolation: the reproductive anatomy 
of one species does not fit with the anatomy of 
another species
○ Example: snails can have varying spirals on 
shells, which prevent mating
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Snail shell/reproductive-anatomy example illustrates mechanical isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Prezygotic Barriers
● Gametic isolation: proteins on the surface of 
gametes do not allow for the egg and sperm to 
fuse
○ Example: the sperm and eggs of red and 
purple sea urchins are released in the water, 
but they cannot fertilize each other
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Sea-urchin gamete example illustrates gametic isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
Take a couple of minutes to review the five types of 
prezygotic barriers with a partner
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Practice Time
Read each example and determine which type of 
prezygotic barrier is at work.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Practice Time
1. Many plants have anatomical structures that only 
allow certain pollinators to collect and distribute 
pollen
a. Answer: mechanical isolation
2. Lions and tigers are both common in India, but 
the lions live in open grasslands, while the tigers 
live in the forest
a. Answer: habitat isolation
3. Female fireflies identify males of their own 
species to mate with by their flashing patterns
a. Answer: behavioral isolation
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Three short scenario prompts test mechanical, habitat, and behavioral prezygotic isolation.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Postzygotic Barriers
● Postzygotic barriers: prevent a hybrid zygote 
from developing into a viable, fertile adult
○ Three types:
■ Reduced hybrid viability
■ Reduced hybrid fertility
■ Hybrid breakdown
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Postzygotic Barriers
● Reduced hybrid viability: The genes of different 
parent species may interact in ways that impair 
the hybrid’s development or survival
○ Example: domestic sheep can fertilize 
domestic goats, but the hybrid embryo dies 
early on
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Sheep-goat embryo example illustrates reduced hybrid viability.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Postzygotic Barriers
● Reduced hybrid fertility: a hybrid can develop 
into a healthy adult, but it is sterile
○ Usually results due to differences in number of 
chromosomes between parents
■ Example: a male donkey and a female horse 
can mate to produce a mule, but mules are 
sterile
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Horse-donkey mule example illustrates reduced hybrid fertility.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Postzygotic Barriers
● Hybrid breakdown: the hybrid of the first 
generation may be fertile, but when they mate 
with a parent species or one another, their 
offspring will be sterile
○ Example: farmers have tried crossing different 
types of cotton plants, but after the first 
generation the plants do not produce viable 
seeds
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Cotton-hybrid example illustrates hybrid breakdown.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Quick Review
Take a couple of minutes to review the three types 
of postzygotic barriers with a partner
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Practice FRQ
Work on the practice FRQ in your packet
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Micro and Macroevolution
● Speciation is a bridge between the concepts of 
microevolution and macroevolution
○ Microevolution: change in allele frequencies 
within a single species or population (natural 
and sexual selection, genetic drift, gene flow)
○ Macroevolution: large evolutionary patterns 
(adaptive radiation, mass extinction)
■ Stasis: no change over long periods of time
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Pace of Speciation
● Evolution and speciation can occur at different 
speeds
○ Punctuated equilibrium: when evolution 
occurs rapidly after a long period of stasis
○ Gradualism: when evolution occurs slowly 
over hundreds, thousands, or millions of years
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Pace-of-speciation comparison contrasts punctuated equilibrium with gradualism.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Evolution and Speciation
● Divergent evolution: groups with the same 
common ancestor evolve and accumulate 
differences resulting in the formation of a new 
species
○ Adaptive radiation: if a new habitat or niche 
becomes available, species can diversify 
rapidly
● Convergent evolution: two different species 
develop similar traits despite having different 
ancestors
○ Analogous traits
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Evolutionary-pattern comparison links divergent evolution, adaptive radiation, convergence, and analogous traits.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Extinction
● Extinction: the termination of a species
● Extinctions have occurred throughout the Earth’s 
history (5 mass extinctions)
○ Human activity has affected extinction rates
■ Anytime there is ecological stress, extinction 
rates can quicken
● If a species does go extinct, it opens up a 
niche that can be exploited by a different 
species
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.
Section-title slide with Earth imagery introduces Origins of Life on Earth.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Origins of Life
● Earth formed approximately 4.6 billion years ago 
(bya)
○ Early Earth was not suitable for life until 3.9 bya
■ Earliest fossil evidence is 3.5 bya
● Cyanobacteria
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Early-Earth timeline text highlights 4.6 bya formation, ~3.9 bya habitability, and ~3.5 bya earliest fossil evidence.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
How Did Life Arise?
● Early Earth contained inorganic molecules
○ These could have synthesized organic 
molecules due to free energy and abundant 
oxygen
■ Organic molecules could have also been 
transported to Earth via meteorites or other 
celestial events
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Primarily text-based instructional slide.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Experimental Data
● Oparin and Haldane 
hypothesized that early 
Earth was primarily 
composed of hydrogen, 
methane, ammonia and 
water
○ Stanley Miller and 
Harold Urey tested the 
hypothesis in their lab
■ They found organic 
compounds and 
amino acids formed
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Miller-Urey apparatus/experiment imagery accompanies the historical Oparin-Haldane hypothesis.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Experimental Data
● Miller and Urey 
hypothesized that the 
organic molecules that 
formed served as the 
building blocks for 
macromolecules
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Experimental-data slide follows the Miller-Urey discussion toward prebiotic building blocks.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
RNA World Hypothesis
● RNA World Hypothesis: proposes that RNA 
could have been the earliest genetic material
○ Helps to explain the pre-cellular stage of life
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: RNA-world slide introduces RNA as a candidate early genetic material.

ppt_raw_slides.raw_text:
Review
Think back to when we covered the endosymbiont 
theory. What was that? How does it relate to this 
topic of the origins of life?
The theory states that mitochondria and chloroplasts 
may have been engulfed by eukaryotic cells.
ppt_raw_slides.visual_content_notes: Endosymbiosis review reconnects earlier Unit 2 content to later eukaryotic evolution.

ced_current_atoms.label: Natural selection as mechanism
ced_current_atoms.statement: Natural selection is a major mechanism that changes populations over generations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Competition and differential reproductive success
ced_current_atoms.statement: When resources are limited, individuals with favorable heritable phenotypes tend to leave more offspring, changing trait frequencies across generations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Evolutionary fitness
ced_current_atoms.statement: Evolutionary fitness is evaluated through reproductive success relative to others in the population.

ced_current_atoms.label: Changing environments change selection
ced_current_atoms.statement: Biotic and abiotic conditions can change, altering which genetic variants are favored and changing the rate or direction of evolution.

ced_current_atoms.label: Selection acts on phenotypic variation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Natural selection acts on phenotypic variation among individuals in a population.

ced_current_atoms.label: Selective pressures
ced_current_atoms.statement: Environmental conditions impose selective pressures that can change over time.

ced_current_atoms.label: Environment-dependent fitness effects
ced_current_atoms.statement: A phenotype can increase or decrease fitness depending on the environment in which it occurs.

ced_current_atoms.label: Molecular variation and organismal fitness
ced_current_atoms.statement: Variation in the number or types of cellular molecules can contribute to differences in survival and reproductive success across environments.

ced_current_atoms.label: Artificial selection
ced_current_atoms.statement: Human selective breeding can change variation and trait frequencies in other species.

ced_current_atoms.label: Random processes in evolution
ced_current_atoms.statement: Random processes can alter the genetic composition of populations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutation adds genetic variation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mutation is a random process with respect to fitness that introduces new genetic variation into populations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genetic drift
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetic drift is a nonselective change in allele frequency caused by chance, especially influential in small populations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Bottleneck effect
ced_current_atoms.statement: A bottleneck is genetic drift following a severe population-size reduction that leaves a nonrepresentative sample of the original gene pool.

ced_current_atoms.label: Founder effect
ced_current_atoms.statement: The founder effect is genetic drift when a new population is established by a small subset whose allele frequencies differ by chance from the source population.

ced_current_atoms.label: Gene flow
ced_current_atoms.statement: Migration of fertile individuals or gametes can add or remove alleles from a population through gene flow.

ced_current_atoms.label: Random processes change allele frequencies
ced_current_atoms.statement: Chance processes can change allele frequencies and thereby contribute to population evolution.

ced_current_atoms.label: Mutation supplies selectable variation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Mutation creates genetic variation that can generate phenotypic variation on which natural selection can act.

ced_current_atoms.label: Drift can drive population divergence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetic drift can make a small population diverge genetically from other populations of the same species.

ced_current_atoms.label: Gene flow counteracts divergence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Gene flow between populations tends to reduce genetic differences and can hinder divergence into separate species.

ced_current_atoms.label: Allele-frequency change as evidence of evolution
ced_current_atoms.statement: A change in allele frequencies across generations is evidence that a population is evolving.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium as null model
ced_current_atoms.statement: Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium is an idealized null model for describing and predicting allele and genotype frequencies at a locus in a non-evolving population; its full set of conditions is not met in real populations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg condition large population
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes a sufficiently large population so random sampling effects are negligible.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg condition no migration
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes no migration or gene flow at the locus being modeled.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg condition no mutation
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes no new mutation changing the alleles at the locus.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg condition random mating
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes random mating with respect to the locus.

ced_current_atoms.label: Hardy-Weinberg condition no natural selection
ced_current_atoms.statement: The Hardy-Weinberg model assumes no differential reproductive success among genotypes at the locus.

ced_current_atoms.label: Allele frequencies from genotype data
ced_current_atoms.statement: Allele frequencies can be calculated from genotype frequencies or genotype counts in a population.

ced_current_atoms.label: Multiple independent evidence streams
ced_current_atoms.statement: Evolution is supported by scientific evidence from many disciplines, including geographical, geological, physical, biochemical, and mathematical data.

ced_current_atoms.label: Extant and extinct evidence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Molecular, morphological, genetic, and fossil evidence from living and extinct organisms informs evolutionary history.

ced_current_atoms.label: Dating fossils
ced_current_atoms.statement: Fossil ages can be inferred using rock context, radiometric methods appropriate to the timescale, and geographic/geologic information.

ced_current_atoms.label: Morphological homology
ced_current_atoms.statement: Homologous and vestigial structures provide evidence of common ancestry.

ced_current_atoms.label: Sequence similarity as evidence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Comparisons of DNA nucleotide sequences and protein amino-acid sequences provide evidence for evolution and common ancestry.

ced_current_atoms.label: Common ancestry of eukaryotes
ced_current_atoms.statement: Shared structural and functional features support common ancestry among eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Membrane-bound organelles as common-ancestry evidence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Shared membrane-bound organelles contribute structural evidence for common ancestry of eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Linear chromosomes as common-ancestry evidence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Linear chromosomes are a conserved feature supporting common ancestry of eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Introns as common-ancestry evidence
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genes containing introns are a conserved molecular feature that contributes evidence for common ancestry of eukaryotes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Evolution continues
ced_current_atoms.statement: All living lineages have evolutionary histories and populations continue to evolve when evolutionary mechanisms change allele frequencies.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genomic change over time
ced_current_atoms.statement: Changes in genomes over generations provide evidence of continuing evolution.

ced_current_atoms.label: Continuity of fossil change
ced_current_atoms.statement: Change observed through the fossil record provides evidence that evolution has continued through time.

ced_current_atoms.label: Evolution of resistance
ced_current_atoms.statement: Resistance to antibiotics, pesticides, herbicides, or chemotherapy drugs can evolve when heritable variants differ in reproductive success under treatment.

ced_current_atoms.label: Pathogen evolution and emerging disease
ced_current_atoms.statement: Pathogen populations can evolve, contributing to the emergence or changing behavior of diseases.

ced_current_atoms.label: Trees and cladograms are testable hypotheses
ced_current_atoms.statement: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms are testable hypotheses about evolutionary relationships among lineages.

ced_current_atoms.label: Tree versus cladogram scale
ced_current_atoms.statement: Phylogenetic trees can represent amounts of evolutionary change or time when calibrated with fossils or molecular clocks; cladograms show branching order without implying scale.

ced_current_atoms.label: Character changes inform phylogeny
ced_current_atoms.statement: Character states that are gained or lost across lineages can be used to infer branching relationships.

ced_current_atoms.label: Outgroup in phylogenetic inference
ced_current_atoms.statement: The outgroup represents a lineage that is less closely related to the focal ingroup than the ingroup members are to one another and helps identify ancestral versus derived character states.

ced_current_atoms.label: Shared derived characters
ced_current_atoms.statement: Shared derived characters support common ancestry and help define clades.

ced_current_atoms.label: Molecular evidence in phylogeny
ced_current_atoms.statement: DNA and protein sequence data generally provide more direct and often more reliable evidence of relatedness than morphology alone.

ced_current_atoms.label: Nodes represent common ancestors
ced_current_atoms.statement: Nodes on phylogenetic trees or cladograms represent inferred most recent common ancestors of descendant lineages.

ced_current_atoms.label: Sources used to construct phylogenies
ced_current_atoms.statement: Phylogenies can be constructed from morphological similarities in living or fossil organisms and from DNA or protein sequence similarities.

ced_current_atoms.label: Phylogenies are revisable
ced_current_atoms.statement: Phylogenetic trees and cladograms are hypotheses that are revised when new evidence changes the best-supported relationships.

ced_current_atoms.label: Speciation requires reproductive isolation
ced_current_atoms.statement: New species can arise when populations become reproductively isolated so gene flow is sufficiently reduced or prevented.

ced_current_atoms.label: Biological species concept
ced_current_atoms.statement: For sexually reproducing organisms, the biological species concept defines a species as populations whose members can interbreed and exchange genetic information to produce viable, fertile offspring.

ced_current_atoms.label: Punctuated equilibrium and gradualism
ced_current_atoms.statement: Evolutionary change can be concentrated in relatively rapid episodes separated by stasis or can accumulate more gradually over long timescales.

ced_current_atoms.label: Divergent evolution and adaptive radiation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Divergent evolution can accompany adaptation to different habitats; adaptive radiation can produce especially rapid diversification when ecological opportunities become available.

ced_current_atoms.label: Convergent evolution
ced_current_atoms.statement: Similar selective pressures can independently favor similar phenotypic adaptations in distantly related populations or species.

ced_current_atoms.label: Allopatric and sympatric speciation
ced_current_atoms.statement: Allopatric speciation involves geographic isolation; sympatric speciation occurs despite geographic overlap.

ced_current_atoms.label: Reproductive isolating mechanisms
ced_current_atoms.statement: Prezygotic and postzygotic barriers can maintain reproductive isolation and reduce gene flow between diverging populations.

ced_current_atoms.label: Genetic variation affects population resilience
ced_current_atoms.statement: The amount and distribution of genetic variation influence population dynamics and the capacity to respond to environmental change.

ced_current_atoms.label: Low diversity increases vulnerability
ced_current_atoms.statement: Populations with little genetic diversity are more vulnerable to decline or extinction when environments change.

ced_current_atoms.label: Diversity increases probability of tolerant variants
ced_current_atoms.statement: Genetically diverse populations are more likely to include individuals whose phenotypes tolerate a novel environmental pressure.

ced_current_atoms.label: Fitness effects depend on environment
ced_current_atoms.statement: An allele that is advantageous under one set of conditions can be neutral or harmful under another because selective pressures differ.

ced_current_atoms.label: Evidence-based origin-of-life models
ced_current_atoms.statement: Models for the origin of life are evaluated using evidence from geology, chemistry, physics, and experiments on plausible prebiotic processes.

ced_current_atoms.label: Geological evidence for origin-of-life timing
ced_current_atoms.statement: Geological evidence constrains models of when and under what conditions life could have originated.

ced_current_atoms.label: Earth and earliest-life dates
ced_current_atoms.statement: Earth formed about 4.6 billion years ago; conditions were too hostile for life until roughly 3.9 billion years ago, and the earliest fossil evidence for life dates to about 3.5 billion years ago.

ced_current_atoms.label: RNA world hypothesis
ced_current_atoms.statement: The RNA world hypothesis proposes that RNA could have served as an early genetic material before modern DNA-protein systems evolved.

ced_current_atoms.label: RNA replication and genetic continuity

ced_current_atoms.label: Base pairing in RNA replication
ced_current_atoms.statement: Complementary base pairing provides the informational template needed for replication in an RNA-world model.

ced_current_atoms.label: Catalysis before encoded proteins
ced_current_atoms.statement: An RNA-world model assumes that genetically encoded proteins were not initially required as catalysts; catalytic RNA could perform some functions.

assessment_semantic_crosswalk.label: Allele versus genotype frequency quick review

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The opening historical sequence can make Darwin’s theory appear to derive mainly from Galápagos observations and uses historical language such as “good,” “bad,” and “improvement.”
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the quote and Galápagos material as historical context. Canonical science must avoid teleology and present natural selection as differential reproductive success acting on heritable variation, with Darwin’s evidence coming from many observations including biogeography, fossils, artificial selection, and species variation.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck says natural selection acts on random mutations, which narrows the target of selection and can imply that mutation alone supplies all relevant variation.
review_flags.resolution: Lock the distinction that mutation is random with respect to fitness and introduces new alleles, while natural selection acts nonrandomly on heritable phenotypic variation. Recombination and sexual reproduction also generate variation from existing alleles.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The sickle-cell example says sickle cell anemia protects against malaria, conflating sickle-cell disease with the heterozygous sickle-cell trait.
review_flags.resolution: Use the heterozygote-advantage framing: in malaria-endemic environments, individuals heterozygous for the sickle-cell allele can have higher fitness than either homozygote. Do not present sickle-cell disease itself as the protective state.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Descent with modification is presented as the modern definition of evolution.
review_flags.resolution: Retain descent with modification as Darwin’s historical framing. For population genetics, define evolution operationally as change in allele frequencies or heritable population characteristics across generations.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck emphasizes traits that lead to survival accumulating in the population.
review_flags.resolution: Use differential reproductive success as the core mechanism. Survival matters when it changes the number of viable offspring contributed to later generations.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The natural-versus-artificial selection slide says both can lead to evolutionary change in the organism.
review_flags.resolution: Canonical wording must state that populations evolve across generations; individual organisms do not evolve genetically during their lifetime.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck groups natural selection with 'random occurrences' that drive evolution.
review_flags.resolution: Separate stochastic mechanisms from selection. Mutation occurrence and genetic drift are random with respect to fitness; gene flow depends on movement; natural selection is nonrandom differential reproductive success among heritable phenotypes.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck states that mutation rates tend to be fast in prokaryotes because of faster generation time.
review_flags.resolution: Distinguish mutation rate per replication from the number of generations per unit time. Short generation times can make evolutionary change appear quickly without implying a universally higher mutation probability per nucleotide per replication.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck states that most mutations fall in the neutral-to-harmful range.
review_flags.resolution: Use a cautious formulation: many mutations are neutral or nearly neutral with respect to fitness, deleterious mutations occur, and beneficial mutations are comparatively rare; the distribution depends on genomic context and environment.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Bottleneck and founder effects are taught as named subtypes of drift but can be mistaken for adaptive processes.
review_flags.resolution: Lock that both are sampling effects that change allele frequencies by chance, can reduce variation, and do not consistently produce adaptation.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Sexual selection is described as males having 'useless structures' simply because females choose them.
review_flags.resolution: Define sexual selection as differential reproductive success arising from mate choice or competition for mates. Sexually selected traits can carry survival costs but are not biologically 'useless,' and mating patterns are not restricted to female choice of male ornaments.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The Hardy-Weinberg sequence implies that violation of any condition necessarily means microevolution and that any genotype-frequency deviation proves allele-frequency evolution.
review_flags.resolution: Treat Hardy-Weinberg as a locus-specific null model. Nonrandom mating alone can change genotype frequencies without changing allele frequencies. A deviation prompts evaluation of which assumptions are violated and whether allele frequencies changed.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck labels p as the dominant allele and q as the recessive allele.
review_flags.resolution: Lock p and q as frequencies of two alleles, with no inherent dominance meaning. Dominance affects phenotype expression, not which symbol must represent an allele.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The problem-solving heuristic treats phenotype or individual-frequency information as automatically equal to p², 2pq, or q².
review_flags.resolution: Only equate genotype frequencies with p², 2pq, and q² under Hardy-Weinberg assumptions. Inferring q² from a recessive phenotype also assumes the phenotype reliably identifies the recessive homozygous genotype.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The genotype-count example takes square roots of observed homozygote frequencies to estimate p and q.
review_flags.resolution: Calculate allele frequencies directly from genotype counts: p=(2N_AA+N_Aa)/(2N) and q=(2N_aa+N_Aa)/(2N). Square-root shortcuts apply only when Hardy-Weinberg genotype proportions are justified.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The diversity slide can be read as 'more diversity is always better.'
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the CED relationship that genetic diversity generally increases the probability that a population contains variants able to withstand a novel pressure, while avoiding an absolute claim that every increase in variation is beneficial.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Carbon-14 is presented as a general fossil-dating method.
review_flags.resolution: Lock radiometric dating to isotope-appropriate timescales. Carbon-14 is useful only for relatively recent organic remains; older fossils are commonly constrained using older surrounding rock layers and longer-lived radioisotopes.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Vestigial structures are defined as structures that no longer have a use, with the human coccyx and appendix as examples.
review_flags.resolution: Define vestigial structures as inherited remnants that have lost much or all of an ancestral function and may retain reduced or modified functions. Do not teach the appendix or coccyx as functionless.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Bird, bat, and bee wings are grouped together as analogous structures without distinguishing the homologous forelimb skeleton of birds and bats.
review_flags.resolution: When discussing flight structures, distinguish analogous wing function from homologous tetrapod forelimb ancestry. Bird and bat forelimbs share homologous skeletal elements even though powered flight evolved independently.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Phylogenetics is defined as a hypothesis of evolutionary history.
review_flags.resolution: Use phylogeny for the evolutionary history/relationship hypothesis and phylogenetics for the methods used to infer and analyze those relationships.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck says phylogenetic trees differ from cladograms because trees show change over time measured by fossils.
review_flags.resolution: Use the current CED distinction: some phylogenetic trees are scaled to time or amount of change and may be calibrated using fossils or molecular clocks; cladograms communicate branching order without a time/change scale.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The term basal taxon can be misread as meaning an extant lineage is primitive or ancestral to other living taxa.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve the classroom term as enrichment but avoid primitive/advanced ranking. A lineage that branches near the root is an extant lineage with an earlier divergence in the represented tree, not the ancestor of the other extant taxa.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Monophyletic/paraphyletic/polyphyletic group labels and the principle of parsimony are taught explicitly, but these exact terms are not required in the current Unit 7 CED.
review_flags.resolution: Retain as teacher-required enrichment. Current AP-required phylogeny focuses on nodes, shared derived characters, outgroups, molecular/morphological evidence, and revisable tree hypotheses.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Parsimony is framed as the rule to use whenever characters conflict.
review_flags.resolution: Teach parsimony as one inference principle that favors fewer evolutionary changes. Modern phylogenetics also uses statistical methods; do not imply parsimony always yields the correct tree.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The biological species definition is presented without its domain limitation.
review_flags.resolution: Apply the biological species concept to sexually reproducing organisms and note that it is difficult or inapplicable for asexual organisms and many fossil taxa.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Sympatric speciation is described as usually resulting from exploitation of a new niche, while allopatric speciation is tied mainly to physical disasters.
review_flags.resolution: Lock geography as the defining contrast. Allopatric isolation can arise through many geographic processes; sympatric speciation can arise through mechanisms such as polyploidy, habitat differentiation, or sexual selection.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Reduced hybrid fertility is said to usually result from differences in parental chromosome number.
review_flags.resolution: Chromosome-number or structural differences can cause hybrid sterility, but genic incompatibilities and meiotic problems can also reduce fertility. Keep the mule as an example without making chromosome number the universal cause.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Hybrid breakdown is defined as later-generation offspring becoming sterile.
review_flags.resolution: Use the broader definition: first-generation hybrids may be viable and fertile, while later-generation hybrids can show reduced viability, reduced fertility, or both.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Divergent evolution is written as if accumulating differences necessarily results in a new species.
review_flags.resolution: Divergence can occur within or among populations and may contribute to speciation when reproductive isolation evolves; divergence does not automatically create a new species.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: Macroevolution, five mass extinctions, and human-driven extinction-rate detail are included beyond the explicit current Unit 7 required statements.
review_flags.resolution: Preserve as teacher enrichment and conceptual context. Do not make memorization of the number of mass extinctions a Unit 7 AP requirement.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The slide labels the earliest 3.5-billion-year fossil evidence as cyanobacteria.
review_flags.resolution: Use the current CED date for earliest fossil evidence without requiring a definitive cyanobacterial identity. Ancient microbial fossils and stromatolites support early life, but assigning all earliest evidence specifically to cyanobacteria is stronger than the CED requires.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The deck says abundant oxygen helped inorganic molecules synthesize organic molecules on early Earth.
review_flags.resolution: Correct this directly. Early Earth had little free molecular oxygen. Plausible energy sources for abiotic organic synthesis include lightning, ultraviolet radiation, volcanism, and geochemical gradients; oxygen was not abundant.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The Oparin-Haldane atmosphere is presented as if its hydrogen/methane/ammonia/water composition is the established composition of early Earth.
review_flags.resolution: Present the strongly reducing atmosphere as the historical hypothesis tested by Miller. Current evidence supports an early atmosphere with substantial nitrogen and carbon dioxide and little oxygen, while locally reducing volcanic conditions may also have occurred.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The Miller-Urey sequence can imply the experiment produced macromolecules or demonstrated the origin of life.
review_flags.resolution: Lock the result to abiotic synthesis of small organic molecules, including amino acids, under simulated conditions. Macromolecule formation, protocells, and self-replicating systems are separate origin-of-life steps.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The RNA-world slide is too brief to cover the current CED requirements.
review_flags.resolution: Add the three AP-required assumptions: RNA replication must permit genetic continuity, complementary base pairing is required for templated replication, and genetically encoded proteins were not initially required as catalysts.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The endosymbiont-theory review says mitochondria and chloroplasts may have been engulfed by eukaryotic cells and can blur organelle origins with the origin of the first life.
review_flags.resolution: Reuse the Unit 2 endosymbiosis lock: mitochondria and chloroplasts descend from formerly free-living prokaryotes incorporated into ancestral host cells. Endosymbiosis explains later eukaryotic evolution, not the initial origin of life.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The bottleneck effect is defined as a drastic reduction caused by a non-selective disaster, which is narrower than the current-CED mechanism and is inconsistent with the slide's inclusion of hunting as an example.
review_flags.resolution: Define a bottleneck as genetic drift following a severe reduction in population size when survivors are a chance, nonrepresentative sample with respect to the focal alleles. A demographic decline can have selective and nonselective components; only the sampling component is genetic drift.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The tree-reading answer labels 'butterflies, moths, and flies' collectively as sister taxa, which can blur the requirement that sister taxa or sister clades are two lineages that share an immediate common ancestor.
review_flags.resolution: Lock sister taxa/sister clades as the two descendant lineages emerging from the same immediate node. In the displayed tree, the butterflies-and-moths lineage/clade is sister to the fly lineage at node C.

review_flags.source_claim_or_issue: The Amish founder-effect example says a small number of founders carried an 'unusual number of mutations,' which incorrectly emphasizes mutation count rather than chance sampling of rare alleles.
review_flags.resolution: Describe the founder effect as a small founding group carrying a nonrepresentative set of alleles, so some rare alleles can become unusually common in the descendant population. Do not imply the founders necessarily had more mutations overall.
